oneSentence: A formally issued or adopted text that sets shared principles, expectations or guidance for behaviour, often without creating the same binding legal duties as a regulation or treaty.
plainExplanation:
A normative instrument is a document that tells people, organisations or States what good practice, expected behaviour or shared principles should look like. In AI governance, it often appears as recommendations, principles, declarations, frameworks or codes issued or adopted by governments or international bodies.

What goes in are negotiations, evidence, political priorities and draft text. Representatives discuss risks, rights, safety, development needs and practical questions. The body then settles or adopts wording through its formal process, which may involve consensus, a vote or another procedure.

What happens next depends on the instrument. Some are legally binding, but many are not. That is why people often call them “soft law”. “Soft law” means a text can still shape behaviour, procurement, standards, funding, reporting and public expectations even if a court may not enforce it in the same way as legislation.

What comes out is a reference point. Governments may use it to design national rules, organisations may use it in internal policies, and technical bodies may align standards with it. It is not the same as a regulation, which creates binding legal obligations, and it is not the same as a resolution, which may record a position, request action or set next steps without setting behavioural standards.

everydayAnalogy.title: A code for the group chat
everydayAnalogy.story: A youth club formally adopts a code for its group chat: do not share another person's details, explain why posts are removed, and provide a way to challenge moderation decisions. The code is not national law, but it shapes what members and moderators are expected to do. Administrators then build its principles into joining instructions, moderator settings and the process for handling complaints. The code sets the direction, while those later measures put it into practice.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A school guide is usually made by one small group and applied in a simple setting. Real normative instruments can involve many States, organisations and stakeholders, long negotiations, careful legal drafting and political compromise. Also, some normative instruments are more formal and influential than a school guide, while others are less precise.

visual.title: How a normative instrument shapes behaviour
visual.learningObjective: Show how negotiated text can influence practice even without operating like a directly enforceable regulation.
visual.description: A left-to-right sequence with four boxes. Read from drafting to adoption to use in practice to downstream effects. Each box shows what enters, what changes and what comes out, so the reader sees why these texts matter even when they are not hard law.

steps.label: 1. Drafting
steps.explanation: States, experts and other participants propose principles, safeguards or guidance on an issue such as AI safety, rights or interoperability.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled Drafting with small input tags: evidence, negotiation, policy goals, stakeholder input.

steps.label: 2. Formal adoption
steps.explanation: A body adopts the text through its process, giving the document political and institutional weight.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box labelled Formal adoption with a document icon and an arrow from Step 1.

steps.label: 3. Use as a reference
steps.explanation: Governments, organisations and standards bodies cite the text when designing policies, procurement rules, internal guidance or future legislation.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box with branching mini-icons for government, organisation and standards body.

steps.label: 4. Behaviour changes
steps.explanation: The text can influence reporting, funding conditions, expectations and later legal or technical rules, even if it does not itself act like a regulation.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth box labelled Behaviour changes with output tags: policy, standards, oversight, practice.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal a short note comparing that step with a regulation, resolution and international standard.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram is a four-step sequence explaining how a normative instrument works. Step 1, Drafting: evidence, negotiation, policy goals and stakeholder input are turned into proposed principles or guidance. Step 2, Formal adoption: an official body adopts the text, giving it authority as a shared reference. Step 3, Use as a reference: governments, organisations and standards bodies use the text to shape policies, internal rules, procurement and future legal drafts. Step 4, Behaviour changes: practice changes through expectations, funding, reporting and later standards or laws. The key message is that influence can be strong even without direct legal enforceability.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the same four boxes in a fixed horizontal line with arrows between them and short captions under each box. No animation; all comparison notes appear as static text below the sequence.

workedExample.scenario: A procurement officer in a country office is revising terms of reference for an AI-assisted search tool covering publicly available documents before the file goes to the procurement unit.
workedExample.input: The office wants to draw on the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, adopted through 41 C/Resolution 15, but the draft terms of reference contain only a general instruction to use AI responsibly.
process: The officer identifies the Recommendation as an adopted normative instrument that sets principles and safeguards, rather than as a procurement rule that applies automatically.
Relevant expectations, such as transparency, human oversight and risk assessment, are translated into evaluation criteria and supplier deliverables.

The procurement unit reviews the resulting clauses under the office's applicable procedures. Once included in the solicitation and contract, those clauses create the specific requirements for the supplier.
The contract manager later records evidence against those requirements in the monitoring report.
workedExample.result: The normative instrument shapes conduct through procurement criteria, contractual clauses and reporting expectations. Its practical influence is real, but the binding supplier obligations come from the contract and applicable rules, not from the Recommendation alone.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: In a documentation and library service, a national officer is checking citations in a statement for delivery before close of business. The draft describes the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence as binding international AI law and is already with the front office for clearance.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The officer corrects the wording to identify the Recommendation as a normative instrument adopted through 41 C/Resolution 15. It articulates principles and safeguards that can shape national policies, organisational rules and procurement practice, without operating in the same way as a treaty or regulation.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Check the adopted text and any legal advice on its status before clearance. Do not describe a recommendation as binding law, or imply that later procurement or reporting requirements flow automatically from it.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, this term matters because many important AI rules do not begin as strict laws. A normative instrument can set expectations early, shape procurement, influence national regulation, guide international cooperation and create a common language for risk, rights and accountability. If you mistake it for a regulation, you may overestimate its legal force. If you dismiss it as “only voluntary”, you may miss how strongly it can still affect funding, standards, organisational behaviour and future negotiations.

In an ICT governance board's first reading of proposed AI guidance
When a procurement unit turns principles into tender clauses

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A normative instrument always means a legally binding law.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not always. Some normative instruments are binding, but many are soft-law texts such as principles, recommendations or declarations. Their effect often comes from political commitment, reputation, procurement choices, standards alignment and later implementation, not only from court enforcement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If it is soft law, it does not matter in practice.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Soft law can matter a great deal. It can shape what governments fund, what organisations report, how vendors design products and what later laws or standards look like. Its influence is indirect, but often real and durable.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A resolution and a normative instrument are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They overlap sometimes, but they are not identical. A resolution is a type of formal decision or expression by a body. A normative instrument is defined by its standard-setting role: it lays out principles, expectations or guidance for behaviour. Some resolutions contain normative language, and some do not.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A normative instrument is just a technical standard.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A technical standard usually specifies detailed methods or requirements so systems can work consistently, for example on testing or interoperability. A normative instrument is often broader and more policy-oriented, covering values, principles, safeguards and governance expectations.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is an official text that tells people what behaviour or safeguards are expected, even if it does not work like a normal law.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In governance practice, a normative instrument is a formally issued or adopted text intended to shape conduct by articulating principles, commitments, safeguards or recommended measures. The category is broader than binding legislation and can include soft-law instruments such as declarations, recommendations, guiding principles, codes or frameworks. Its practical effect often travels through national policy uptake, organisational rules, procurement conditions, reporting expectations, administrative reference, donor requirements and alignment with technical standards. A regulation is a binding rule adopted by a recognised authority. A resolution is a formal text through which a body may record a position, request action or set next steps. An international standard is agreed by a recognised standards body and sets common technical or organisational requirements for consistency. Usage can vary across institutions, so the exact legal status depends on the issuing body, mandate and text.

keyTakeaway: A normative instrument sets an agreed direction for conduct. Its effect often comes through later policies, contracts, procedures and reporting requirements, rather than direct legal enforceability.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a normative instrument in AI governance?
options: A document that always creates directly enforceable legal penalties for non-compliance
A formally adopted text that sets principles or guidance and may influence behaviour even without acting like a direct regulation
A private technical manual used only by software engineers
A vote record showing which Member States supported a meeting agenda
quickCheck.explanation: The best answer is the second one. A normative instrument sets shared expectations or standards for behaviour. It may be legally binding in some cases, but often it works through guidance, political commitment, procurement, standards and later policy uptake rather than direct enforcement.

contested: The label and scope are somewhat unsettled across institutions. Some users apply it broadly to many standard-setting texts, while others reserve it for more formal instruments or distinguish sharply between binding and non-binding forms.

issues.problem: The page inconsistently treats formal adoption as necessary. The technical definition correctly allows a normative instrument to be issued or adopted, but the one-sentence definition and process diagram allow only adoption. A formally issued code or framework would be excluded.
issues.fix: Use “formally issued or adopted” in the definition. Rename Step 2 “Formal issue or adoption” and say that a body issues or adopts the text through its relevant process.

issues.problem: “Representatives ... then agree wording” wrongly suggests that adoption requires representatives to agree. A body may adopt wording through a vote or another formal procedure without consensus among its representatives.
issues.fix: Replace that sentence with: “The body then settles or adopts wording through its formal process, which may involve consensus, a vote or another procedure.”

issues.problem: The claim that regulation “usually denotes directly applicable legal rules backed by a defined enforcement regime” is too specific and is not supported by the supplied definition. A regulation is binding, but whether it is directly applicable and how it is enforced depend on the legal system. The paragraph also fails to distinguish an international standard accurately.
issues.fix: Define regulation as a binding rule adopted by a recognised authority. Define an international standard by its recognised standards body and its common technical or organisational requirements, rather than merely calling it detailed.

issues.problem: The distinction from an international standard is weak and partly inaccurate. International standards can cover organisational requirements as well as technical methods, and they need not be described simply as detailed. The defining distinction supplied for this page is that they are agreed by a recognised standards body to support consistency.
issues.fix: An international standard is agreed by a recognised standards body and sets common technical or organisational requirements so products, services or processes work consistently. A normative instrument is the broader governance category described here and often sets principles, commitments or safeguards.

issues.problem: The marked answer is the only reasonable answer, but the distractors are implausible caricatures. Option 1 says “always” and requires penalties, option 3 is restricted to private engineering manuals, and option 4 is merely a vote record. A learner can answer without distinguishing a normative instrument from a regulation, resolution or international standard.
issues.fix: Replace the distractors with: “A binding rule from an authority, with legal duties for those it covers”; keep the marked option; “A standards-body document for consistent products, services or processes”; and “A formal assembly text recording a position, request or next step”.
